newsitem.title: CROATIA: Zagreb government rows back on radio shutdown.
newsitem.headline: Zagreb government rows back on radio shutdown.

text.p: Taken aback by sharp international criticism and mounting dissent at home, the Croatian government on Thursday started rowing back on its bid to shut down an influential independent radio station.

The United States and Britain had sharply criticised the Zagreb government's move against Radio 101 and in Croatia itself, a prominent human rights activist called for a mass street demonstration in the capital.
After the protests, the head of the state-controlled telecommunications council said it would open a new tender for the radio frequency it withdrew from independent Radio 101 on Wednesday.
Radio 101 will continue its regular broadcasting until the council reaches a new decision, council head Branko Mocibob was quoted as saying by state radio.
The owner of a rival station which obtained Radio 101's frequency said in a statement earlier that he was renouncing the concession "in favour of Radio 101".
The council announcement came only hours after both government and ruling Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) party officials voiced their support for the popular radio station.
Radio 101, founded in 1984, was one of the prime promoters of peaceful changes that led to the country's first democratic elections in April, 1990.

President Franjo Tudjman won that poll and led the nation to bloody secession from Yugoslavia. Since then he has been criticised for ruling the country with an authoritarian hand, clamping down on political opponents and independent media.
In a statement following a regular cabinet session, the government said that "all conditions are met for opening a new tender to award (a broadcasting licence for the Zagreb) radio frequency".
The HDZ city comittee also called on the council to "reconsider its decision and find a satisfactory solution".
The sudden change of mind was clearly caused by international reaction and domestic protests which grew into a wider demand for democratic reforms.
The United States and Britain criticised the crackdown against Radio 101 and urged the government to reconsider.
"This development in the case of Radio 101 constitues a significant setback for democratisation and free expression in Croatia," said U.S. State Department spokesman Glyn Davies.
In Croatia, a prominent human rights activist called for a mass street demonstration in the capital.

Ivan Zvonimir Cicak, head of the Croatian branch of the human rights watchdog Helsinki Committee (HHO), called on radio listeners to gather at the capital's main square on Thursday night in support of Radio 101.

In a statement broadcast on the radio, the HHO urged people to gather in the central Ban Jelacic square and light candles, recalling the peaceful protests that brought down communist rule in Croatia in late 1989 and early 1990.
"Use the candle flames to light the path of democracy in Croatia," Cicak told the radio.
The government decision caused an avalanche of protests and expressions of support from public figures, including ruling party members, soldiers and Zagreb residents.
The station aired telegrams of support late into the night and on Thursday morning, when the state telephone company complained that it had been flooded with calls.
"The political atmosphere in Zagreb now is similar to that in 1989," independent commentator Davor Gjenero said, referring to the times when communism was crumbling in former Yugoslavia.
"There is a lot of frustration against the authoritarian or totalitarian type of government. The Radio 101 is just a symbol," Gjenero told Reuters.
President Tudjman, who has been receiving treatment at a U.S. military hospital near Washington, was due to return to Croatia on Friday, according to his private doctor.
